A composite index combines several acoustic measures into one score through a
regression equation fitted on one cohort. The [AVQI](avqi.qmd) combines six
measures, computed on a concatenated sample of continuous speech and sustained
vowel, into a score for overall voice quality [@barsties2016avqi]. The
[ABI](abi.qmd) combines nine measures on the same kind of sample into a score
for breathiness [@delgado2018avqi; @barsties2021abi]. Both run from 0 to 10
[@maryn2010ecological; @barsties2021abi].

The two chapters on the indices describe each one in detail. This chapter
collects what applies to both and is easy to miss when each is read alone. Its
argument fits in one sentence: **a composite threshold is a property of a whole
configuration, and every part of that configuration has been shown to move
it.** For the software side of the argument, see
[Pipeline dependence](foundations-pipeline.qmd).

## The equation is the measure

A composite score is defined by its published coefficients. Anyone can
implement the equation from the paper, which is what keeps the AVQI and the ABI
algorithm-defined measures rather than model-derived ones in this reference's
compatibility rule (see [Pipeline dependence](foundations-pipeline.qmd)). The
corollary is that the version of the equation is part of the measure.

**Versions are different measures.** AVQI versions 02.02 and 03.01 differ in
the length of the continuous-speech part, 17 against 34 syllables in Dutch, and
in the regression weighting [@barsties2016avqi]. Across the studies pooled in
the AVQI meta-analysis, the mean threshold was 3.05 (± 0.22) for version 02
and 2.22 (± 0.52) for version 03 [@jayakumar2024avqi]. A version 02.02
threshold, such as the Japanese 3.15 [@hosokawa2017avqi], cannot be compared
with a version 03.01 one.

**Version labels do not reliably identify the equation.** A technical note
labels the development study's equation version 2.03, and says the later
Praat-only equation was cited both as 02.02 and as 2.06 [@zainaee2025note]. Its
own authors had reported version 2.06 in a Persian validation but had used 2.03
[@zainaee2025note]. A second Persian validation, by a different group, reports
AVQI 03.01 computed in VOXplot, but the equation it prints is the development
study's, with its ×2.571 rescaling [@aghajanzadeh2025persian;
@maryn2010ecological]. The paper does not let a reader tell whether the
equation or the version label is the error.

**Printed equations differ.** Two validations misprint the AVQI 03.01 HNR term,
and one also the Tilt coefficient; two print the ABI intercept with a different
digit string. The [AVQI](avqi.qmd) and [ABI](abi.qmd) chapters tabulate these
and say which reading this reference follows. The practical rule is the one
those chapters give: take the coefficients from the script the developers
published, not from an equation retyped in a later paper.

## What moves a threshold

There is no single threshold for either index. A threshold belongs to an index
version, a language and its speech material, a reference standard, a
derivation criterion, a sample and a software pipeline. Each of these has been
shown to move it.

| What changes | Everything else held fixed? | What happens | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Index version (AVQI 02 against 03) | no: pooled across studies | mean threshold 3.05 against 2.22 | @jayakumar2024avqi |
| Speech material: counting 1–11 against reading text, same 53 speakers | yes | AVQI 1.16 → 1.56; ABI 2.38 → 3.13 | @englert2020material |
| Reference standard: breathiness B against overall grade G, same sample | yes | ABI 3.66 against 3.41 | @jayakumar2024abi |
| Reference standard: GRBAS breathiness against CAPE-V breathiness, same sample | yes | ABI 3.75 against 2.97 | @lucero2026phonalab |
| Derivation criterion: Youden index against 95th percentile of controls, same sample | yes | AVQI 03.01 1.41 against 2.06 | @hosokawa2019avqi |
| Praat version: 6.0.46, with a CPPS bug, against unaffected versions; same recordings and script | yes | at the German thresholds, sensitivity falls from 72% to 23% (AVQI) and to 9% (ABI) | @stappenbeck2020praat |
| Language | no: samples, pipelines and standards differ too | AVQI 03.01 from 1.16 to 2.43; ABI from 2.35 to 3.69, across the language validations | @englert2020material; @castillo2023avqi; @barsties2016avqi; @barsties2021abi |

: What moves a composite threshold. One documented case per factor. This is a map of what moves a threshold, not a table of cutoffs; the cutoffs, with their Pipeline and Class cells, are in the [AVQI](avqi.qmd) and [ABI](abi.qmd) chapters. {#tbl-composite-drift}

The rows marked "yes" isolate one factor each, and they are the informative
ones. The language row does not isolate anything: every pair of language
validations also differs in sample, reference standard, derivation criterion
and usually software. The spread across languages therefore cannot be read as
an effect of language alone.

::: {#cell-fig-composite-drift .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}
panels = [
    ("AVQI 03.01", (1.16, 2.43), [
        ("Derivation criterion\n(Japanese)", 1.41, 2.06, "Youden", "95th pct", vs.ORANGE),
        ("Speech material\n(Brazilian Portuguese)", 1.16, 1.56, "counting", "reading", vs.BLUE),
    ]),
    ("ABI", (2.35, 3.69), [
        ("Reference standard\n(PVQD, American English)", 2.97, 3.75, "CAPE-V B", "GRBAS B", vs.GREEN),
        ("Reference standard\n(Malayalam, Kannada)", 3.41, 3.66, "grade G", "breathiness B", vs.GREEN),
        ("Speech material\n(Brazilian Portuguese)", 2.38, 3.13, "counting", "reading", vs.BLUE),
    ]),
]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.6, 3.4),
                         gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1, 1.15]})
for ax, (title, band, rows) in zip(axes, panels):
    ax.axvspan(*band, color=vs.GRID, alpha=0.9, zorder=0, lw=0)
    for i, (label, a, b, la, lb, c) in enumerate(rows):
        y = len(rows) - 1 - i
        ax.plot([a, b], [y, y], color=c, lw=2.0, zorder=2, solid_capstyle="butt")
        for x, lab, ha, dx in ((a, la, "right", -0.04), (b, lb, "left", 0.04)):
            ax.plot([x], [y], "o", ms=6, color=c, markeredgecolor="white",
                    markeredgewidth=0.8, zorder=3)
            ax.text(x + dx, y + 0.18, f"{x:.2f}", color=c, fontsize=7.5,
                    ha=ha, va="bottom")
            ax.text(x + dx, y - 0.2, lab, color=vs.MUTED, fontsize=7,
                    ha=ha, va="top")
    ax.set_yticks(range(len(rows)), [r[0] for r in rows][::-1])
    ax.set_ylim(-0.75, len(rows) - 0.35)
    lo, hi = band
    ax.set_xlim(lo - 0.45, hi + 0.45)
    ax.set_xlabel("threshold (index points)")
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.text(hi, len(rows) - 0.42, "range of language thresholds",
            color=vs.MUTED, fontsize=7, ha="right", va="bottom")
    vs.style_axes(ax, grid=False)
    ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0)
fig.tight_layout()
```

**Pooled values are not cutoffs.** The ABI meta-analysis derived a weighted
threshold of 3.40 across six studies, with pooled sensitivity highly
heterogeneous (*I*^2^ = 89.7%) [@barsties2021abi]. Pooled AVQI version 03
sensitivity was even more heterogeneous (*I*^2^ = 95.3%) [@jayakumar2024avqi].
A pooled threshold averages over exactly the factors in @tbl-composite-drift.
This reference reports such values as context and never as a cutoff.

## What "validated" means

**Development figures overstate accuracy.** The 60-sample study that produced
the AVQI 03.01 weighting reports, at a threshold of 2.43, a sensitivity of
1.00 and a specificity of 0.936 [@barsties2015consistency; @barsties2016avqi].
That threshold was evaluated on the same samples that fitted the weights. On
1058 new samples the same threshold gave a sensitivity of 0.785 and a
specificity of 0.932 [@barsties2016avqi]. A perfect sensitivity in a
development sample is a sign of where the number came from, not of how the
index will perform. The candidate cutoffs in the PhonaLab study of the PVQD
were checked against this by repeated ten-fold cross-validation, with AUC
optimism of 0.002 or less [@lucero2026phonalab].

**External validation, as the developers defined it.** @barsties2016avqi
define external validity as the ability to reproduce results with alternative
subjects and in settings outside the initial study, and tested the AVQI on a
completely new and independent set of voices and judges. The later studies are
of a different kind. They validate the indices in new languages and derive a
new threshold in each [@barsties2021abi; @barsties2020german]. A threshold
re-derived in a new sample is a new estimate, not a replication of the old one.

**How independent the evidence is.** Of the thirteen development and
language-validation studies in @tbl-composite-authors, ten include an index
developer, Barsties v. Latoszek or Maryn, among their authors. The
exploratory PVQD candidates are not a validation and are not counted; their
author developed PhonaLab [@lucero2026phonalab].

| Study | Index | Language | Developer among authors |
|---|---|---|---|
| @barsties2016avqi | AVQI | Dutch | yes |
| @barsties2017abi | ABI | Dutch | yes |
| @delgado2018avqi | both | Spanish | yes |
| @barsties2020german | both | German | yes |
| @pommee2020avqi | AVQI | French | yes |
| @englert2020material | both | Brazilian Portuguese | no |
| @englert2021avqi | AVQI | Brazilian Portuguese | yes |
| @hosokawa2019avqi | AVQI | Japanese | yes |
| @hosokawa2019abi | ABI | Japanese | yes |
| @castillo2023avqi | both | US English | yes |
| @kankare2023abi | ABI | Finnish | no |
| @jayakumar2024abi | ABI | Malayalam, Kannada | no |
| @aghajanzadeh2025persian | both | Persian | yes |

: Developer authorship of the AVQI and ABI validations in this reference's sources, from the papers' author lines. {#tbl-composite-authors}

One corpus of 218 German recordings underlies the German validation, the
Praat-versions study and the VOXplot single-measure study
[@stappenbeck2020praat; @barsties2023voxplot]. The ABI meta-analysis counts
among its authors the first authors of five of the six studies it pools
[@barsties2021abi]. None of this makes a result wrong, and developer
involvement is how a protocol gets followed faithfully in a new language. It
does mean that agreement among these studies is weaker evidence than the
number of studies suggests.

**Base rates.** The Dutch external validation sample was 8% normophonic and
92% dysphonic. The authors used likelihood ratios because they are less
vulnerable to such base-rate differences than ROC statistics alone
[@barsties2016avqi]. Sensitivity and specificity from a sample that skewed are
a poor guide to a clinic's own mix.

## How the indices relate

**Shared construction.** Both indices are computed on voiced segments of
continuous speech, extracted automatically and concatenated with a sustained
vowel [@barsties2016avqi; @barsties2021abi]. Both depend on a balance between
the two speech types: the AVQI 03.01 weighting was built for it
[@barsties2015consistency], and the ABI meta-analysis treated unequal
proportions as a risk of bias [@barsties2021abi].

**Shared components, different targets.** Three of the six AVQI measures are
also ABI measures: CPPS, shimmer local and shimmer local dB
[@barsties2016avqi; @delgado2018avqi]. In the AVQI, CPPS is the main factor
[@barsties2016avqi]. But the AVQI estimates overall voice quality, judged as
GRBAS grade [@barsties2016avqi], and the ABI estimates breathiness and suits
voices dominated by it [@barsties2021abi]. The two scores are not
interchangeable, and neither is a substitute for the other.

**What a composite adds over its best component.** In the PVQD, the ABI
outperformed HNR for breathiness on a DeLong test, but not CPPS: AUC 0.862
against 0.843, *P* = 0.209 [@lucero2026phonalab]. In the developers' pooled
comparison of indices, AVQI 03.01 had the highest concurrent validity with
perceived overall voice quality, weighted *r* = 0.821, against 0.524 for the
Dysphonia Severity Index and 0.788 and 0.748 for the Cepstral Spectral Index
of Dysphonia on vowels and on speech [@barsties2016avqi]. Whether a composite
earns its extra measures over CPPS alone is a question to ask of each sample,
not a settled fact. The DSI has no chapter of its own yet, because its
development paper is not among this reference's sources.

## Software and recording

**Praat versions.** One Praat version, 6.0.46, carries a CPPS bug that cut
sensitivity at the German thresholds to 23% for the AVQI and 9% for the ABI,
while correlations with perceptual ratings stayed intact
[@stappenbeck2020praat]. The details are in
[Pipeline dependence](foundations-pipeline.qmd).

**Software other than the Praat scripts.** Several recent validations computed
both indices in VOXplot [@castillo2023avqi; @kankare2023abi;
@aghajanzadeh2025persian], which uses the Praat algorithms for signal
processing behind its own interface [@barsties2023voxplot]. The ABI
meta-analysis excluded studies that did not use Praat with the customised
script [@barsties2021abi]. No study among this reference's sources compares
VOXplot with the Praat scripts on the same recordings.

**Sampling rate.** The French AVQI validation recorded at 11,025 Hz
[@pommee2020avqi], while the AVQI script computes spectral slope and tilt over
bands reaching 10 kHz [@barsties2016avqi]. See the [AVQI](avqi.qmd) chapter.

## Reading or reporting a composite score

Every factor in @tbl-composite-drift has to be known before a score can be
compared with a threshold. A report of an AVQI or ABI score should therefore
state:

1. the index and its version, and where the equation was taken from;
2. the software and its version, and the script version where there is one;
3. the language, the speech material and the number of syllables of
   continuous speech;
4. for any threshold applied: the study it comes from, its reference standard
   and its derivation criterion.

A threshold whose study differs from the measurement on any of these is not a
cutoff for that measurement. This list is this reference's recommendation,
drawn from the sources above, not a published standard.

## Where the sources disagree

**Are the indices robust across languages?** @delgado2018avqi found the
Spanish AVQI threshold close to the Dutch and Japanese ones and suggested that
the AVQI may be relatively insulated from inter-language phonetic differences.
The ABI meta-analysis found the ABI relatively robust to phonetic differences
such as stress timing, syllable timing and intonation [@barsties2021abi].
Later validations widened the ranges to 1.16–2.43 for the AVQI 03.01 and
2.35–3.69 for the ABI [@englert2020material; @castillo2023avqi;
@barsties2016avqi; @barsties2021abi].
Those validations also differ in speech material, reference standard,
derivation criterion and software, each of which moves a threshold on its own.
Whether the remaining spread reflects language is therefore not established.
This is this reference's reading of the sources together.

**Which Japanese threshold.** @hosokawa2019avqi computed 1.41 by the Youden
index and 2.06 by the 95th percentile of controls, and recommend 2.06. Most
other language rows are Youden-derived, so the Japanese row reflects a
different criterion as well as a different language. The [AVQI](avqi.qmd)
chapter keeps 2.06 and flags it.
